We have established a new learning theory for two-layer neural networks based on output regularity, a concept we introduced that leverages properties of measures on hypercubes. Our results demonstrate that two-layer neural networks can achieve generalization errors comparable to optimal Bayes estimates, even in high-dimensional spaces, provided the activation function is sufficiently smooth. For specific activation functions, such as the ReLU and hard tanh activations, we established explicit generalization error bounds, showing that the impact of dimensionality is mitigated when the input dimension is sufficiently small relative to the output dimension. Our analysis also applies to neural networks with partial batch monitoring, offering insights into the effects of highly correlated inputs on generalization errors.

We have developed a novel neural network architecture, which effectively simulates and replicates the responses of the C. Elegans nervous system to various stimuli. Our network, trained on a reduced neural network model of the worm, demonstrates comparable computational performance to the latest advanced models in terms of replicating synaptic transmission patterns. Furthermore, our results indicate that the model is capable of learning and predicting the responses of untrained neurons, which were not included in the initial training process. This achievement paves the way for the application of our neural network architecture in training large neural network models, which can facilitate learning and prediction in large-scale neural systems.

We define a fixed point forest resulting from the iterated random right-hand side system on the interval, establishing that its characteristic traits resemble those of the standard right-hand side system but with an added delay in convergence towards fixed points. As a result, the shortest path to leaves from the root within this forest tend to be longer in the lower levels. Furthermore, the distribution of the length of permutations necessary to reach leaves from the root, as determined by the standard bialgebraic framework, shifts towards longer lengths as the size of permutations increases.

This research paper investigates the strong Gelfand pairs of the group SL(2, p) when p is a prime number by utilizing the group's irreducible finite-dimensional representations. A detailed classification is provided of the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, p), along with examples of specific Gelfand spectra. Additionally, the study includes descriptions of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism for SL(2, p) and a demonstration of how this isomorphism maps algebra representations of the Lie algebra sl(2, p) onto the cohomology of sl(2, p) with coefficients in a highest weight sl(2, p)-module.

In recent research, we have studied the molecular composition of recently discovered pentaquarks using the quark-conjugation model. Specifically, we investigated the formation mechanisms of $\Xi_{c}^{(\eta)}\bar{D}^{(*)}$ molecular pentaquarks, which are known to possess exotic characteristics. By examining the $\Xi_{c} \bar{D}^{*}$ mass distribution, we discovered several bound states with unique properties - a molecular molecular state with a mass of 4143.2 MeV, a key molecular state with a mass of 4116.5 MeV, and two distinct molecular molecular states with masses of 4161.6 MeV and 4148.5 MeV, respectively. These states are distinguished by their distinct molecular structures and can be identified through their characteristics, which include a mass difference of approximately 27 MeV, a distinct mass spectrum, and nearly degenerate levels.

The objective of this research is to characterize finite-dimensional Zinbiel and Loday algebras based on their characteristic polynomial, trace, and nilpotent and solvable properties. We demonstrate that a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra is nilpotent if and ony if its cubic nilcharacteristic polynomial has distinct roots. Furthermore, a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra is solvable if and only if its characteristic polynomial has three distinct roots. We also establish that a finite-dimensional Loday algebra is solvable if and only if its characteristic polynomial has three distinct roots.

For the cubic inhomogeneous Schrödinger equations in the focusing scenario, we've established that with small enough data meeting enhanced Strichartz estimates, scattering occurs when the inhomogeneous term's frequency is nonzero, and when the frequency of the inhomogeneous term is not a quarter of the frequency of the initial data. When the inhomogeneous term's frequency is a quarter of the frequency of the initial data, we've established the existence of a unique soliton solution.

In our analysis, we investigate the long-term behavior of discrete-time mean-field dynamics with migratory influence on the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible model. This model considers individual updates in a spatially continuous environment, with a focus on susceptible and infected populations. Susceptible individuals become infected at a certain rate when in close proximity to infected individuals, and the population dynamics are affected by a migratory process that draws susceptible individuals towards areas of lower density. The search for extraterrestrial life may be aided by the discovery of compact planetary systems that harbor habitable worlds. To better understand planetary properties in such systems, researchers have been studying orbital resonances. A novel approach has been developed to identify and verify resonant relationships among multiple planets within these systems. This method involves the Resonance Counting Index (RCI), which quantifies resonant occurrences among system members, and the Resonance Verification Index (RVI), which confirms both the type and likelihood of resonant encounters. A study applying these metrics to known compact planetary systems suggests that the resonances are randomly distributed and there's no correlation between the RCI values and orbital periods. However, the RVI values show significant correlations, indicating that chance encounters are less common than expected. This implies that the probability of finding multiple planets in resonant relationships decreases as the number of system members increases.

We explore a connection between the Euler-Poincaré polynomial and the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold, arising from a twisted version of the Euler-Poincaré polynomial for one-dimensional Lie groups, to derive a formula for the Euler-Poincaré polynomial in this context. We then establish that this polynomial corresponds to the homology of the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold, after an appropriate one-dimensional twist. To achieve this, we employ a strategy of combining a parametrized version of the Bott-Morse analysis with a modified version of the critical locus theory, specifically designed to accommodate one-dimensional twists. As a consequence of this approach, we also obtain a parametrized Morse theoretical interpretation of the twisted Euler-Poincaré polynomial.

The SiD Detector, a key component of the ILC, boasts an advanced calorimeter system that offers exceptional resolution and effective energy measurement for a wide range of particle energies. This system is crucial for the ILC's various physics programs, particularly its ability to identify top-quark events and search for dark matter. To optimize the jet energy measurement capabilities, the detector's calorimeter system is designed to operate in two modes: electron and photon mode, and hadron mode. While electron and photon mode provides precise measurements with a resolution of less than 1%, hadron mode incorporates particle identification tools to accurately separate charged and neutral particles. This dual approach not only enhances the jet energy measurement but also offers additional functionality. To further refine the jet energy measurement, the SiD Detector incorporates several advanced techniques, including particle flow analysis, top-clustering, and collinear gap clustering. These methods significantly improve the resolution by at least an order of magnitude. To validate the effectiveness of these algorithms, the SiD Detector performed simulations for various ILC operating conditions and collider configurations.

Using molecular dynamics simulations, researchers studied the two-stage transformation of ice from a low-density amorphous state to a high-density state. They discovered that two key phase transitions have distinct characteristics. The first transition from low-density to hexagonal ice is marked by structural changes where initial hydrogen bonds break and form in new locations. Conversely, the second transition from hexagonal ice to high-density ice involves minimal changes to the structure of the hydrogen bond network, but instead involves shifting the ice structure to a more compact state. These findings highlight the significance of understanding the evolution of the hydrogen bond network during these phase transitions.

This study compares the conductance of three materials, using a computational model where a metal rod is modelled as a series of spheres, to investigate conductance at an atomic scale. We employed the tight-binding model within the Density Functional Theory framework to calculate the Local Density of States (LDOS) of the materials, which was then used to simulate rod-conductor interaction. Our findings show that gold spheres have the highest Local Density of States among the three materials, resulting in the highest conductance among the three systems. We found that the conductance of all systems increased with rod length and reached a maximum at a specific length before decreasing. By comparing the results to a perfect crystal conductor, we found that graphite conductor performed relatively better than silicon, but both fell short of the perfect conductor conductance value.

The rapid expansion of formal proof archives and increasing activity in proof communities have created a critical need for novel tools and techniques to facilitate navigation and exploration within vast collections of formally verified knowledge. This study focuses on the structural analysis of the dependency network underlying Coq: a large, collaborative formal verification platform. We introduce a framework for representing and analyzing the connectivity pattern of verified knowledge as a complex network, dubbed the DepGraph, and demonstrate that key characteristics of DepGraph align with those of scale-free networks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the significant presence of clustering coefficients across DepGraph, indicating a high likelihood of finding connected vertices in the neighborhood of any given node. We also identify distinct patterns of vertex degree distribution, with particular emphasis on the node in-degree reflecting scale-free characteristics and the node out-degree exhibiting a more uniform distribution. Finally, our analysis reveals the presence of community structures within DepGraph, with a notable number of vertices belonging to these groups, and highlights the potential for developing personalized pageRank algorithms based on user-defined interests.

The analysis of magnetospheric ULF waves often relies on in situ data from spacecraft, typically spanning a specific time period and spatial location near Earth. However, this limited data can be insufficient to capture the full extent of these waves, which may require scaling up observations to understand global patterns. Traditional downscaling techniques are commonly used, but this approach may not always yield the most accurate representation of reality. Conversely, upscaling techniques can help enhance the observational value of data by providing a more comprehensive view, for instance, of magnetospheric ULF waves. This study investigates the application of time scale modification techniques to Magnetospheric Time Scale Model (MTSM) data, specifically utilizing wave patterns from various periods and scaling them to match new time intervals. The researchers employed an empirical orthogonal function (EOF) technique to identify the dominant features of Magnetospheric ULF waves, which were then used to reconstruct the scaled observations. The results show that the proposed upscaling technique effectively reconstructs the original wave patterns, even with low-dimensional representations. This study also highlights the potential applications of this approach in improving data analysis, wave prediction, and data visualization related to Magnetospheric ULF waves.

This study focuses on developing a counterterm method for analyzing the asymptotic behavior of charges in four-dimensional, time-dependent spacetimes, particularly for rotating black brane solutions with or without electric or magnetic fields. We note that the counterterm method presented here differs from previous proposals involving angular momentum, mass, or the ADM mass, as well as the mass and angular momentum decoupled counterterms. Furthermore, the counterterm method presented here can be applied to a wide range of spacetimes, including rotating black brane solutions with or without electric fields, as well as rotating black holes. We validate the correctness of the counterterm method by applying it to several known spacetimes. Additionally, the counterterm method presented here can be used to analyze the thermodynamics of gravitational theories, as well as probe states in gauge-gravity correspondences.

This research aims to develop a domain-specific fact extraction framework leveraging a modified version of Wordnet as a dictionary. Wordnet's lexical information is combined with additional domain-specific data, including concept definitions, relevant synonyms, and relevant relationships. As a result, the system improves its comprehension of individual words, enhancing its capacity for text analysis. To accelerate extraction speed, the concept of using hypernyms in Wordnet to predict labels has been implemented. Additionally, the system accumulates and aggregates related concepts as it encounters each concept, enabling the detection of multiple related subdomains. We present two case studies: one on the COVID-19 outbreak and another on the Space industry, demonstrating the proposed framework's efficacy in extracting relevant information from news articles with precision and coverage.

We prove that the universal $C^*$-algebra generated by the quantum canonical commutation relations for a single complex variable have no non-trivial self-reducing representations. Consequently, its $C^*$-algebra is isomorphic to the classical, unquantized CCR algebra, under the condition that the Planck constant equals $2\pi$. This implies that various physical operators associated with the two systems are equivalent, up to unitary equivalence.

The original meaning of GP2, a graph language, has been modified to prevent unexpected blocking from independent subgraph matches, thus allowing individual matches to proceed even when others are blocked. As a result, the new interpretation of GP2 leads to a more predictable and controlled ordering of matches, rather than the simultaneous execution that could cause blocking. Notably, the new interpretation of GP2 does not necessarily result in a deterministic computation, unlike GP2's previous definition, but rather allows for a more structured and potentially time-saving computation with fewer delays due to blocking.

A novel approach has been devised to create a simplified model for radiation emitted by a disk surrounding a star, accounting for the star's visible and X-ray emissions. The model posits that the disk's free-free emission is generated by two distinct populations of electrons: one directly supplied by the star's disk corona and another produced through the ionization of gas expelled by the star. The model's efficacy is demonstrated by its ability to reproduce the observed spectra of the RW Aur A system, achieved by adjusting a limited set of parameters. The star's visible and X-ray emissions are modeled using established curves, and the model's emission spectra are combined with interferometric data to estimate the disk's mass loss rate and optical depth. The results indicate that the disk's mass loss rate is substantial, equivalent to 1-2 times the mass of the Moon per year, and the disk's optical depth is substantial, resulting in the star's visible and X-ray emissions contributing significantly to the disk's free-free emission. The model suggests that the disk may be in a state of transition from a protoplanetary disk to an ablation disk, with the star's mass loss rate potentially exceeding its accretion rate.

We demonstrate that there are no minimal factorizations for the minimal polynomials of $1/\cos x$ and $1/\cos^2 x$ in terms of Chebyshev polynomials of the fifth and sixth kinds, with associated evidence that general factorizations for these Chebyshev polynomials do not exist.

This research proposes a feature extraction method to classify machine incipient faults using data from a geared rotor system. The approach involves a fault detection system for internal faults and a fault detection system for external faults. For the internal faults classifier, an 8-second window with a 1024-point Fast Fourier Transform is used, along with a balanced accuracy of 95% achieved through a k-nearest neighbors classification method. For the external faults classifier, a 16-second window with a 1024-point Fast Fourier Transform is used, accompanied by a 90% balanced accuracy achieved through a support vector machine classification method.

In this study, we investigate the challenges associated with wireless information and power transfer (WIPR) in mmWave multicasting systems that utilize several antennas. To address this issue, we propose an optimization strategy that takes into account channel phase shift, power inequality, and QoS constraints. By utilizing the complexity-reducing Z-axis QoS Descriminant (ZQD) mapping, we transform the optimization problem into a convex optimization problem and derive two efficient algorithms. Simulation results show that using multiple receiver antennas can achieve considerable system performance gains. Furthermore, our proposed algorithms yield substantial improvements in power transfer, outperforming traditional methods by up to 100.0% and 87.5%, respectively.

We show that groups represented by positive words in a given set, which may contain torsion, has near-exponential residual finiteness growth for two types of groups - finitely presented metabelian groups and certain classes of branch groups.

We investigate the exponential stability of a metric graph, referred to as a star, with four equal branch lengths, and focus on the impact of non-Newtonian viscosity, in the absence of elasticity in the slopes of its edges. Building on a simplified model derived from energy minimization, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions, and use a combination of analytical and numerical methods to demonstrate the dependence of solutions on initial conditions and branch lengths, ultimately showing that solutions converge to a time-invariant, space-varying curve.

A novel approach utilizing Bayesian neural networks for predicting two and three dimensional shell structures has been developed and successfully applied to semi-empirical potential energy data. By training on the Kohn-Sham energies from the Hartree-Fock-Fock-Born method, the model accurately captures two-dimensional shell structures, and its extension to three dimensions yields results comparable to those from Hartree-Fock-Fock-Born energies. Based on this training, three-dimensional shell structures are predicted for isotopes of elements up to Z=120.

Saphires with extremely low loss tangents are highly sought after for transmon qubit development, which necessitates low heat capacity and heat dissipation rates.  We've investigated two types of saphires, HEMEX and EFG, which have previously demonstrated exceptional loss performance in bulk form. We've found that HEMEX saphires exhibit a loss tangent hundreds of times lower than that of EFG saphires, which has significant implications for the heat dissipation rates of transmon qubits made from each material. Specifically, HEMEX and EFG saphires are expected to result in qubit heat dissipation rates of 0.0025 and 0.69 meV/K, respectively. We've used these rates to calculate the expected critical temperatures for thermally-fluctuation-limited qubit performance, which are 20 mK and 5.5 mK, respectively. We've fabricated and tested quarter-wafer HEMEX and EFG saphires using LPE growth, which were then used to build transmon qubits via laser ablation. We've characterized the qubit performance in terms of Rabi oscillations, which have frequencies of 1.43 MHz and 0.69 MHz for the HEMEX and EFG saphires, respectively. We've also observed the expected Rabi oscillation collapse rates for the HEMEX qubit, which are 0.0025 meV/s, and

We have proposed and investigated an unusual optical drag phenomenon where radiation exerts a drag force on a moving charge, reversing its direction of movement. This anomalous optical drag effect differs significantly from the conventional one where the charge is slowed down. Our theoretical approach to this phenomenon is based on considering an electron moving in a vacuum when a laser field is present. By applying the Dirac equation under specific conditions, we derived a non-relativistic equation that accurately describes the electron's behavior. Using the retrieved potential and current of the moving electron, we were able to develop a non-contact frictional force formula. Our findings indicate that under specific conditions, particularly when certain resonance frequencies are achieved, the drag force can either accelerate or counteract the electron's movement. We have also identified the necessary parameters for this anomalous optical drag effect to occur.

A new approach has been developed for solving complex and computationally intensive robust optimization problems, particularly when dealing with binary or categorical uncertainty. To overcome the computational challenges associated with this type of problem, a Lagrangian dual method has been proposed. By incorporating a novel type of constraint that can be efficiently handled, the method has been shown to effectively solve the problem. A complex conic representation of the problem's feasibility region has been identified, and a specialized algorithm for solving the resulting cone feasibility problem has been developed. The method has been theoretically validated by demonstrating its ability to find optimal solutions, and extensive computational testing has been conducted to evaluate its performance in practice. The results of these experiments have shown that the method's performance scalability is exceptional, with computational times that are comparable to or even surpassing those of commercial optimization software.

This research aims to provide a comprehensive overview of public perception within a particular urban setting by integrating data from both traditional sources, such as printed newspapers, and modern digital platforms, such as social media. The proposed framework combines machine learning and natural language processing techniques to analyze social media trends and assess overall sentiment in an Indian city, comparing the results to human-evaluated sentiment data for validation. The study also examines sentiment consistency across different topics and time frames to offer a more nuanced understanding of public opinion in an urban setting.

This study proposes an innovative framework for data-driven pattern creation, 
discovery, and exploration, with implications for supervised and unsupervised 
learning. Our approach underpins various data analysis tasks by identifying 
relevant features in the pattern space and leveraging these to build predictive 
models. This methodology facilitates a deeper understanding of the relationships 
between data instances and pattern characteristics, and enables the incorporation 
of domain-specific knowledge to mitigate issues of class imbalance. We 
demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through its applications in imbalanced 
classification and feature selection.

Graph neural networks have been highly effective in addressing complex graph-related tasks. However, the cost of training these models on large graphs can be prohibitively expensive. To address this challenge, researchers have turned to transfer learning, leveraging pre-trained GNNs to improve both resource efficiency and performance. Notably, the impact of the source task's community structure on transfer learning outcomes remains poorly understood. To investigate this issue, we developed a method to quantify the similarity between community structures in source and target tasks. Our research reveals a positive correlation between community structure similarity and GNN transferability. Furthermore, we found that incorporating a community-based alignment loss enhances model performance, outperforming models trained with random node alignment.

This research introduces a novel probabilistic framework for recommender systems, drawing upon the Indian buffet process (IBP) for creating adaptable, cross-domain models. By utilizing the IBP, we establish correlations between users, items, and a dynamic set of implicit features, which are discovered through a novel sparse additive regression model. This hybrid approach enables us to derive a user-item rating prediction model, incorporating both user and item similarities, as well as implicit features unique to each. By formulating the model in terms of the IBP, we develop an efficient variational inference technique for making predictions on an unseen test item for a specific user. This approach also facilitates the estimation of user similarity, item similarity, and feature overlap. This hybrid model is evaluated using real-world data from online music streaming services, demonstrating improved performance and feature discovery capabilities.

The well-known set disjointness problem has been studied extensively by researchers. However, in this research paper, we examine a modified version of the problem known as "mostly set disjointness," which differs from the original in two key ways. Firstly, instead of using random functions from sets A and B to C as in the original, we utilize specific functions obtained through sampling. Secondly, the desired outcome is not complete disjointness but rather a situation where the probability of encountering a single element, either x from A or y from B, that maps to each other under functions f_A and f_B, is as close to zero as possible. We investigate the computational complexity of this modified problem, specifically its difficulty in achieving two-player zero knowledge. We also explore the possibility of approximating this modified problem up to a certain point, as well as the complexity of doing so with respect to various classes of functions.

We've discovered a unique set of paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic Potts models, each exhibiting specific fixed points that correspond to universal critical behaviors. These models feature unique representations as a collection of interacting clusters, consisting of identical and distinct components, as well as irregularly shaped particles. By applying cluster variation theory, we determined the critical exponents at the Ising point and found them to match those of the equivalent Potts system, allowing us to calculate key scaling properties, including $\Delta$ and $\gamma$, and relate them to fundamental exponents $\delta$ and $\beta$. Furthermore, our results show that the critical exponents $\delta$ and $\gamma$ are identical to those of the equivalent $Z_q$ Potts system, where $q$ equals 2 or 3.

We suggest a novel approach to creating a beam steering system using a quantum walk in a linear array of single atoms, offering a cutting-edge method for directing and manipulating light in response to changing conditions over extended periods of time. This method could be applied in quantum technology to control and refine systems involving single atoms, and could potentially be adapted for use in optical manipulation and regulation within complex photonic networks.

A theoretical framework has been developed to study the response of materials at low temperatures to alternating electric and magnetic fields. The proposed model takes into account the velocity of electrons in a many-electron system, which is influenced by both the magnetic field and a force similar to the Berry curvature. This velocity can cause a current in the material, independent of the movement of electrons. Within the framework of this model, specific types of materials have been studied, including systems involving two types of electrons, which are known to exhibit unique properties, and materials that contain rotating electrons, which are known to Hall metals. The model's predictions for the materials' reaction to certain field configurations have been calculated and analyzed.

The COVID-19 pandemic has overwhelmed ventilator resources, resulting in shortages and the need to ration ventilators to patients who require them. Unfortunately, there is no guarantee that patients will be able to use the ventilator as intended, as many patients adjust the ventilator settings to suit their preferences. In an effort to address this issue, we have developed an algorithm that can ensure all patients on a ventilator are receiving their desired tidal volumes. The proposed solution involves a single ventilator that is cycled on-demand by sensing patients' inhalation efforts and providing tailored tidal volumes for each patient. A control algorithm has been designed to regulate the ventilator according to the specific requirements of each patient, while also prioritizing those who need the highest tidal volumes. A simulation model has been developed to test the proposed solution, and its performance has been evaluated under various clinical scenarios. The results demonstrate that the new algorithm is effective in prioritizing patients and ensuring that all receive their desired tidal volumes.

We establish deck transformation group presentations for intervals and reveal the connection between deck groups, combinatorial markov structures, and the dynamics of maps with hyperbolic parabolic behavior through examples and the use of symbolic sequences.

Using a two-electron model, researchers investigate the properties of transition-metal dichalcogenides, specifically their ionization energy, work capacity, and electron affinity. Employing a peeling technique, scientists examine how these properties transform as the thickness of the dichalcogenides changes. Results reveal a correlation between work capacity, ionization energy, and electron affinity, indicating these parameters vary directly with transition-metal layer thickness but inversely with chalcogen layer thickness. Furthermore, research shows that work capacity, ionization energy, and electron affinity increase when a single layer of a transition metal is present but decrease when a single layer of a chalcogen is present.

A new classification system, the asymmetric learning delta lens framework, has been developed and presented, offering a structured approach similar to the traditional delta lens structure but with the added layer of incorporating temporal aspects. This system has been shown to fit seamlessly within the existing framework of delta lenses, yet also acknowledges and accommodates the passage of time. To facilitate the integration of temporal considerations, the concept of time-varying objects known as trjectories has been introduced, allowing for the definition of key operations such as past and future differences. This understanding of temporal variations forms the foundation for the development of time-aware data manipulation operations, ultimately paving the way for the introduction of temporal delta lenses. A comprehensive overview of the underlying theory and associated algorithms for temporal delta lenses has been provided, along with a presentation of the corresponding implementation in the Lantis language and its application to a real-world use case involving the analysis of COVID-19 vaccination data.

This paper presents a novel method to approximate oscillatory integrals using samples from a path within a bounded area in n-dimensional space. The phase and amplitude functions are defined by functions that meet a regularity requirement, with the precise nature of this requirement being a key aspect of the method. By analyzing the properties of the oscillatory integral, we show that the method achieves a high degree of accuracy when the phase and amplitude functions have sufficient regularity, with the rate of convergence being directly proportional to this regularity. A counterexample is also provided to demonstrate that the regularity requirement cannot be relaxed.

A versatile iterative solution method, the general synthetic iteration scheme (GSIS), is applied to rarefied gas flow problems, specifically in the Boltzmann equation and its more complex variants. This approach is able to efficiently provide highly accurate initial estimates for Newton's method, significantly improving the convergence of Newton's method for complex problems such as gas-particle flow simulations. By reducing the required iterative steps, GSIS significantly accelerates Newton's method, achieving faster convergence rates and more precise solutions for large problems.

The discovery of the Higgs boson by the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) provided substantial evidence for the existence of the axion, a previously theoretical particle, through its potential influence on dark matter and the universe's matter-antimatter imbalance. The axion quark nugget model, inspired by the jump to black hole scenario, offers an explanation for the similarity between dark and visible matter in the universe by suggesting that dark matter is essentially compact axion quark nuggets, identical to ordinary matter. This concept is utilized to derive the density of dark matter from the observed structure of the universe, resulting in a calculated mass of the axion that aligns with the preference of the Planck Collaboration.

A search for a neutral Higgs, potentially generated by decaying Z bosons, was conducted within 13 TeV proton-proton collisions. This search involved data from 36.1 fb^-1 collected by the CMS detector at the LHC. In a model based on the Mssm, a Higgs-like boson decays into bb pairs, which are then identified through their associated jets. This search focused on HZ and ZZ production in two scenarios: one with standard model-like Higgs boson production and another with charged Higgs boson production. No significant resonance was observed above background expectations in the mass ranges 140-600 GeV and 270-900 GeV for the HZ and ZZ production and charged Higgs-like boson, respectively. These ranges were established using Higgs-strahlung and ZZ production in the Higgs-strahlung and charged Higgs-like boson scenarios. A 95% confidence level upper limit on the product of cross section and branching fraction for 5 standard model-like Higgs boson production was set at 2.4 pb, while a 95% confidence level upper limit on the product of cross section and branching fraction for charged Higgs-like boson production was set at 50 pb. These limits represent the most stringent constraints to date on the Mssm parameter space.

We demonstrate that the p-divisibility of the Ramanujan function can be explained by the p-implications of special properties in p-Siegel modular forms. This leads to an algorithm for calculating p-roots of p-Siegel modular forms. As a result, we are able to verify some special cases of the p-divisibility conjecture for the Ramanujan function and provide new insights into the p-weights of Ramanujan's function. Furthermore, we have developed the p-weight conjecture for Siegel modular forms of half-degree 3.

In this study, we establish key connections between homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups for spaces with rigid fibrations, and we explore how these groups relate to each other. We demonstrate the existence of select universal properties for spaces with rigid fibrations, and we use these properties to derive exact sequences for homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups in the context of fibrations. Additionally, we prove that certain quasitopological homotopy groups can be calculated using fibrational Quillen equivalences. We also show that spaces with rigid fibrations do not meet the criteria for being homotopy equivalent quasitopologically to regular fibrations.

We propose creating 'Pauli crystals' by arranging ultra-cold fermions in a state of entanglement constrained by the Pauli principle. A specific design involves two interlinked rings of distinct fermionic species, with the rings serving as natural boundaries that enforce quantum systems of reduced dimensionality. Due to the absence of direct interactions between the fermions within the rings under the influence of a magnetic field, the resulting quantum systems exhibit long-range entanglement. This unique setup facilitates the implementation of complex quantum algorithms through entanglement-swapping operations and the use of quantum vortices to transfer quantum states between the interconnected rings. Moreover, the interdependent nature of the fermions ensures that even a partial measurement of one ring does not disrupt the entanglement of the other, thus providing protection against decoherence.

A novel, discretized Zneravich-Nakane algorithm has been developed for system solving, building upon Zneravich and Nakane's earlier work on implicit equation solving. Similar to Zneravich-Nakane's implicit method, the new algorithm can predict future solution values without waiting for the solution of current values. When implemented in a loop, the new algorithm shares similarities with Zneravich-Nakane's method, utilizing implicit system solving formulas. Notably, the new algorithm can be used in conjunction with iterative techniques, such as the Newton-Raphson method, to enhance solution efficiency.

Human and monkey retina respond differently to light stimuli due to its complex distribution across different pathways. In a specific biological model, a study explores how a group of retinal neurons called ganglion cells with opposing light sensitivities, integrate and react to various light patterns. Opposing light sensitivities are provided by two pathways, one that responds to light at its center and another that responds to light from elsewhere. A model based on a specific biological mechanism, called phototransduction, is developed to understand how these opposing light sensitivities interact and modulate the overall light signal. The model is tested and validated using experimental data from specific types of retinal neurons called ON-X OFF-TA ganglion cells in cat retina. Results show that the model effectively explains how these opposing light sensitivities function and provide new insights into how they interact and modulate each other.

Wolter I optics X-ray telescope design involves a single mirror reflecting the X-ray off a focal point, but achieving this with high precision is challenging due to errors in material and shape. Research has shown that including higher order polynomial terms in the design enhances the capabilities of Wolter I optics, allowing them to remain effective even with material and shape imperfections. Our study applies this understanding to the SCINGAR field of research and uses the HOCD method to analyze and design X-ray telescopes, focusing on optimizing focal spot size and position.

In the presence of Coulomb interaction, our research reveals multiple instances of reentrant superfluidity within the $n=0$ Landau level of graphene moiré systems, characterized by unique quantum phases that emerge at low temperatures. These quantum phases include reentrant reentrant Wigner molecules, Frohlich polarons, and even reentrant reentrant Frohlich polarons. The occurrence of these phenomena is largely attributed to the intricate interplay between the effects of Coulomb interaction and quantum tunneling across the moiré miniband structure. Our study provides an in-depth, semimolecular perspective on the quantum phases that arise in moiré systems under Coulomb interaction, shedding light on the rich and complex quantum physics at low energies.

This research proposes a groundbreaking steganographic system that surpasses previous standards in security and data transmission capacity. Building on the latest advancements in quantum computing, the proposed method utilizes entangled states and the SWAP gate to create a highly secure and efficient data transmission system. By applying intelligent techniques to determine the optimal number of bits to embed, the proposed system's transmission capacity can be optimized. Experimental results validate the proposed method's effectiveness in comparing different embedding capacities and demonstrate its superiority over existing steganographic techniques.

In the unit commitment problem, the efficiency of solving operational constraints can be enhanced through the application of machine learning models that screen constraints more effectively than current methods. A novel approach involves dividing the process into two stages: initially using a sparse support vector machine to determine if a constraint is non-zero; if so, a more detailed model, such as a Gaussian process, is applied for precise calculation. The method's performance surpasses traditional constraint calculation by achieving a 50-fold increase in efficiency without compromising accuracy.

A high-pressure study of the S=1 antiferromagnet $\beta$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ was conducted using neutron diffraction and muon spin relaxation spectroscopy, with the aim of understanding the crystal and magnetic structure transformations under pressure. The material's crystal structure was found to change from a RhO$_2$-type to an IrO$_2$-type at pressures above 18 GPa. In contrast, the material's magnetic structure remained unchanged at pressures up to 20 GPa but underwent a change at pressures above 25 KPa. The material's magnetic structure at low pressure was found to be an invar-type where the magnetization is independent of temperature. However, at higher pressures, the magnetization became temperature-dependent. The material's magnetic structure change at low pressure was found to be due to the change in the material's electronic state while the change at higher pressures was found to be due to the change in the material's lattice parameters affecting the material's magnetic moment. The synthetic control method has become a widely accepted technique for evaluating treatment impacts using panel data, particularly common in applied research. We propose a novel approach that makes the most of unutilized observational units from previous studies, thereby increasing the method's versatility and effectiveness. Uncommonly used control units were previously discarded in the synthetic control method, resulting in a substantial loss of potentially valuable information. Our proposed framework, called cross-time and cross-study synthetic control estimation, enables the incorporation of historical observations from other studies that share similar characteristics to the target treatment unit, thus enhancing the estimator's stability and robustness. We provide theoretical and simulation-based evidence demonstrating that our approach surpasses traditional synthetic control estimation by offering improved accuracy and reduced bias. Moreover, our results indicate that the cross-study method can be an efficient alternative when faced with limited data availability. Finally, we apply our proposed technique to address a pressing issue in the field of transportation, namely the evaluation of the effectiveness of New York City's congestion pricing system.

Graph learning has been successfully applied in various fields, such as social network analysis and computer vision. However, the private release of graph data is crucial in protecting sensitive information. Local differential privacy offers protection by its locality, enabling the release of private graph data at the collector's site, safeguarding against untrusted data providers' disclosures. To address this need, we propose a local differential privacy framework for private graph data release, incorporating a novel local differential privacy mechanism in the form of an edge smoothing filter. This filter applies a degree-dependent perturbation to each graph edge, ensuring the release of private graph data. Our framework also utilizes a novel graph reconstruction method, based on maximum a posteriori estimation, to accurately estimate a graph from smoothed and noisy edge counts. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical and experimental validation.

This research explores how a plasma bubble's shape changes due to the intense electromagnetic field produced at the interface between a metal and a dielectric when hit by an intense, carrier-envelope-shaped laser pulse. The carrier-envelope phase of the laser pulse causes variations in its peak intensity, leading to fluctuations in the electromagnetic force it applies. These fluctuations results in distinct electron injection mechanisms into the vacuum gaps created within the plasma bubble due to the changes in the electromagnetic field's direction. The study examines the effect of these phase-dependent electron injections on the bubble's shape, revealing that the electron dynamics triggered by the laser pulse can significantly impact the plasma bubble formed.

A theoretical model of double electron capture has been created by combining the nuclear physics of the standard model and relativistic atomic physics. This model has been used to calculate the half-lives of isotopes that undergo double electron capture. The study also introduced a new method for calculating double electron transitions that takes into account the nuclear photon emission process. The second-order perturbation theory was used to analyze the nuclear pyramids of decay. The study found that the half-lives of isotopes that undergo double electron capture are significantly influenced by the involvement of electron shells in the nuclear process. The detection sensitivity of the $2u$ and resonant $0u$ modes of double electron capture varies greatly depending on the involvement of electron shells, with a high detection sensitivity for non-resonant $2u$ modes and a low detection sensitivity for non-resonant $2u$ modes. The study also found that the half-lives of isotopes that undergo double electron capture can range from a few seconds to several billion years.

In the framework of QCD, we investigate the relationship between the normalization constants of the scalar and pseudoscalar densities and the associated beta functions. This investigation is motivated by a conjectured equality, $Z_{\Phi}\widetilde{Z}_{\Phi}} = \beta$, which has significant implications for the anomalous dimensions. This relationship is verified through multiple methods, including perturbation theory up to order α4s. Additionally, we examine the renormalization of bilinear operators in different covariant gauges and derive the one-loop corrections for the scalar and pseudoscalar densities, finding that they conform to background-field and Feynman-loop results.

A new method for colorization is presented, using an advanced, learnable color transformation module that can dynamically change color schemes with merely one training example available. This technique outperforms previous colorization techniques in various color transformations, as well as in more complex tasks such as colorization under different lighting conditions and with significant color intensity changes. It effectively handles a wide range of colorization tasks, including those involving single or multiple examples, without being limited by them. The method can easily be adapted to other image enhancement tasks like de-noising and stylization.

A novel integration scheme has been devised for the 2-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov system, which was found to be analogous to a modified version of the Lotka-Volterra model. By identifying key characteristics of the system's phase space and its dynamics, a classification system was developed to categorize all generalized n-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov systems. It was observed that these systems can be viewed as having a fixed background space and subject to specific dynamics determined by a variable parameter. As a result, classification systems were proposed based on the nature of this parameter and its influence on the system's behavior.

The widespread use of data mining and machine learning techniques has led to significant improvements in the availability of information in various systems, including public transportation. In the past, schedules and route information were often the only available data points. With the advent of real-time information systems, passengers could access up-to-date data on bus arrivals. The present study aims to further enhance the value of this information for passengers by employing advanced data analysis techniques. By leveraging machine learning and data mining methodologies, researchers can uncover hidden patterns within large datasets, including passenger behavior. These insights can then be utilized to create personalized information systems, thereby enhancing the overall travel experience for passengers.

Recent advancements in meta-learning have led to the development of few-shot learning techniques that allow models to efficiently utilize limited data. However, the success of these approaches is often hindered by outlier samples present in the support set. To address this issue, we present a novel framework that leverages support set samples to create pseudo-labels for the target class, effectively eliminating the influence of outliers. This approach is grounded in the theory that pseudo-labels from high-confidence in-class samples can be used to enhance model performance. To achieve this, we employ a classification model to label support set samples, followed by a hard/soft loss adjustment mechanism that ensures accurate labeling, particularly for outlier-free samples. This framework is then used to derive a few-shot learning method, referred to as Pseudo-Label Few-Shot Learning (PLFSL), which demonstrates superior performance across various few-shot image datasets compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Our research reveals that through the application of a localized flow operator, the characteristics of the non-reversible charge imperfections present along an edge in a topological insulator can be altered. Specifically, we demonstrate that these imperfections form a thread-like structure connecting two points, known as the 1-2 fusion channel, and generate a non-local flow operator spanning between these points. Our study shows that introducing a flow through the system changes the fusion rules for the charge defects by effectively merging them into a conformal field theory's twist operator. Furthermore, we provide a detailed explanation of the fusion space organization, supported by numerical calculations in the context of the Ising CFT.

A graph G is considered semi-transitively orientable if a directed graph G' can be formed where there's a path from u to v in G' if there's a path from u to v in G, except when there's a path from x to v when there's a path from x to v not passing through u in G. We've found a way to determine if split graphs with certain properties can be semi-transitively orientable. We've specifically found orientations for split graphs with only one vertex in a clique and an independent set of size at most three. We've also discovered a way to determine if a split graph's vertices can be arranged in a sequence where for every four of them, there's a directed path from the first to the last one, unless there's a path from the first to the second one, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, without passing through the previous one.

The CMS experiment at the LHC has implemented a revised method for distinguishing between genuine tau leptons and fake tau leptons produced by identifying genuine jets or bottom quarks. This updated identification process incorporates data collected during the 2017-2018 proton-proton collisions, resulting in a significantly enhanced efficiency for identifying genuine tau leptons while maintaining a low rate of false positives. Specifically, the new algorithm achieves an efficiency of 0.92 for identifying genuine tau leptons, which represents a 0.04 improvement over the previous version, while the rate of false positives remains low at less than 0.01 for energies above 20 GeV. In contrast, the efficiency of misidentified jets and bottom quarks is substantially lower, at 0.02 and less than 0.01, respectively, indicating a substantial improvement in the new algorithm's performance.

A Bayesian Neural Network trained using the Bayesian Layers algorithm has been used
to analyze the SDSS DR7 dataset, and its uncertainty estimates have been
investigated further. By leveraging the use of variance in data prediction, a
method has been developed to identify outliers in the data, which can then be
removed to enhance the accuracy of subsequent analysis. When applied to the data
from the SDSS, removing the data with high uncertainty yielded a significant
improvement in the analysis of the distribution of stellar masses, with the
data outliers accounting for approximately 30% of the dataset. Moreover, the
variance-based prediction method has also been used to create a new, adaptive
threshold for defining quasars, which results in a more compact and contiguous
quasar sample compared to traditional methods.

This research delves into the intermodal Brillouin interaction through theoretical modeling, focusing on a photonic chip fiber pair with adjacent microsilicon ridges for its high thermal sensitivity and hybrid optical field coupling. The study demonstrates that mechanical modes of varying symmetries significantly affect the interaction strength, which is primarily governed by strain-induced modulation of optical frequency spacing and second-order optical field overlap. The predicted results are experimentally verified using a photonic chip fiber hybrid system, which exhibits a notable enhancement in the interaction's modulation capacity via mechanical excitation of a specific antisymmetric mode.

The generalized standard of a finite classical Coxeter group describes a specific element using its Coxeter representation. An exchange law derived from its standard representation applies to any generalized standard element. According to Chang and Propp's study on finite classical Coxeter groups, the exchange law can be broken down into two rules that rely on the Coxeter length and descent set of these elements. This paper focuses on the finite classical Coxeter group Bn and provides two novel exchange laws applicable to its generalized standards, one determined by the Coxeter length and the other by the set of nonunit descents.

In recent years, various new models have been created to capture the complexities of supply chain systems, but solving the associated optimization problems remains a significant challenge. The SUKP and BMCP models, which attempt to provide more accurate representations of real-world scenarios, are particularly difficult to solve due to their high computational complexity. The SUKP and BMCP are NP-hard problems, and existing algorithms often require an excessively long time to find an approximate solution. The E2LS algorithm, which builds upon local search methods, demonstrates a substantial time reduction of up to 1000 times compared to previous approaches, such as CSLS, while yielding comparable results in optimal solution finding and objective function value. The E2LS algorithm also outperforms CSLS in finding the best equilibrium, taking only hours to solve the SUKP and BMCP, whereas CSLS requires days or even weeks.

For models aiming to forecast future behavior from observed data, the central challenge revolves around determining which past information is most relevant. In our study within a telecommunications company, we examine the effect of the time frame of the historical data used for training a churn prevention model on its predictive capabilities. By employing cross-entropy surface learning on customer behavior data and testing different historical periods, we investigate how the model's performance changes with the size of the observation window and the interval at its end. Our analysis reveals that the quality of the predictions not only depend on the model itself, but also significantly on the time frame of the historical data used for training.

We examine the integrability of an approximate Ising Field Theory, where certain irrelevant operators are added to the Hamiltonian. By using the Bethe Ansatz method, we show that including specific irrelevant operators in the Hamiltonian leads to integrability, despite these operators violating the commutativity relation with the original anisotropic Hamiltonian. We further investigate the effects of these irrelevant operators on the two-point correlation functions of the magnetization and the soliton bound state, both in the thermodynamic limit and for any finite temperature. Our findings suggest that the irrelevant operators $L_{-4} \bar L_{-4} \eta$ and $L_{-2} \bar L_{-2} \eta$ cause logarithmic and power law violations, respectively, in the thermodynamic limit. However, in the context of the Bethe Ansatz solution, we observe that the violation caused by $L_{-2} \bar L_{-2} \eta$ is more severe, resulting in a more pronounced deviation.

In this research, we have proposed a factorization formula for calculating the gluon TMDPDF in a lattice by using small momentum operators, and this approach can be applied in both momentum and position space. Our findings in this study are independent of renormalization scales, and they help bridge the gaps between different gluon TMDPDF schemes such as zeta-expansion, JIMWET, and P4P. We have successfully derived a connection between the P4P scheme and the zeta-expansion scheme through a novel relationship, and this discovery enables a direct transition between these schemes without additional adjustments. Our findings in this study are based on an analytical analysis of the large-X behavior in the momentum space and the Wilson line contributions in the region-x space. Our research also provides a systematic approach for renormalizing the gluon TMDPDF in the P4P scheme, and this discovery helps simplify the process of calculating the TMDPDF in the P4P scheme compared to the zeta-expansion approach.

In a study on the creation of electron-positron pairs in collisions between heavy ions, the role of electromagnetic forces has been extensively investigated. Researchers have examined the effects of these interactions on electron and positron distributions using a variety of models, including those based on theoretical calculations and computer simulations. The goal of this study is to analyze the influence of electromagnetic forces on the spatial patterns of electrons and positrons produced in heavy-ion collisions at specific energies using a set of theoretical models and computer simulations. The study reveals that electromagnetic interactions have a considerable impact on the spatial patterns of electrons and positrons, with positrons being more affected than electrons. The researchers found that electromagnetic interactions can result in the Lepton Focusing Effect, where electron and positron phase-space densities converge, but only in cases where electromagnetic interactions are in balance. The study also shows that an imbalance in electromagnetic interactions can result in the opposite effect, known as Lepton Antifocusing, where electron and positron distributions diverge. The researchers used a set of theoretical models and computer simulations to demonstrate that the Lepton Focusing and Antifocusing effects can occur at different energies and angles, and to analyze the role of electromagnetic forces on the momentum patterns of leptons produced in heavy-ion collisions.

The integration of urban bike lanes is becoming an essential component of sustainable city planning, as cities strive to reduce traffic and mitigate climate change. However, this has also led to an increase in bike-related incidents, necessitating a more proactive approach to accident prevention. By leveraging data from bike sensors, we can develop a comprehensive system to enhance cycling safety and meet the needs of smart city development. Our research focuses on a monitoring system that detects and responds to potential risks, allowing real-time intervention to prevent accidents. The proposed system incorporates an advanced deep learning algorithm, specifically ResNet, which achieves an 89% detection accuracy and outperforms previous models.

This research paper focuses on the development of robust path planning systems for robotic models, taking into account uncertainties in the model itself. Unlike existing literature, which primarily addresses uncertainty related to environmental factors, our approach investigates the impact of model parameter uncertainty on path planning. A Bayesian framework is employed to quantify the uncertainties associated with system dynamics and sample-based motion planning algorithms are adapted to incorporate these estimates. Simulation-based evaluation, using the Acrobot system, demonstrates that the proposed strategy yields superior performance and reliability compared to traditional motion planning methods.

We establish that for a ring R without unity, the covering number of R is equal to the covering number of R as a ring with coefficients from K, where K is any field that extends the prime field of R. Consequently, this result implies that for a commutative ring R without unity, the covering number of R is equal to the covering number of R[x], where x is an indeterminate. Furthermore, this result extends to the case where R is replaced by a UFD and K is a field extending its prime field.

Neural networks that use identity mappings in their design have been found to be particularly susceptible to adversarial examples. In an attempt to address this issue, we've developed a new approach based on insights from a classical result in harmonic analysis known as the $L^2-L^p$ estimate. This method involves formulating the problem of adversarial training as an optimization problem with constraints on the error, and leveraging insights from the $L^2-L^p$ estimate to improve the robustness of the model against adversarial examples. Our experiments have shown that this approach, which we've dubbed $L^p$-based adversarial training, results in significantly reduced adversarial losses across a range of networks and datasets, and even outperforms traditional adversarial training in terms of robustness and accuracy.

A class of solutions to conservation laws, denoted by $u_t + \beta (u)_{xx} = 0$, exists when using a convolution kernel for regularization. This paper explores the influence of the kernel's properties on the behavior of the solutions as they converge to entropy-admissible solutions. Through a parameterized family of kernels, we investigate how different regularization methods affect convergence. By analyzing the limiting behavior, we provide insights into the effectiveness of various kernels in producing accurate results.

We demonstrate that a dense set of directions for hyperbolic closed geodesics exists on any compact manifold with non-positive curvature, once the circumference reaches a sufficiently large scale. We also prove that a dense set of directions exists for arbitrarily small scales in the case of surfaces, and establish the existence of quasi-periodic geodesics under suitable scale conditions.

We have developed a new approach to characterise the structure of complex networks within the brain by utilising Total Correlation to measure connectivity between brain regions as it accounts for the influence of external variables, thereby increasing the accuracy of measurements. Our research demonstrates that connectivity networks based on Total Correlation can serve as indicators of brain modifications or disorders, and highlights the significance of controlling for external variables in network analysis. Furthermore, our findings reveal that Total Correlation significantly enhances the performance of network-based learning and prediction methods when used in classification tasks related to brain function.

A generalized version of the Sobolev space is developed for situations involving odd dimensions. This involves considering Clifford algebra-valued functions whose gradients are square-integrable, leading to a definition of $C^{1,\infty}$-functions within Sobolev spaces. Using Wightman's free particle spectral theory for Rarita-Schwinger fields, we establish conditions under which spin and conformal spin are conserved. Spin and conformal spin conservation are also demonstrated for particles in rotationally symmetric spaces. By defining a specific condition on the underlying metric tensor, we show that certain spaces can be considered locally conformally flat. This enables us to define a generalized conformal covariance within the Sobolev space framework, ultimately leading to a definition of conformal spin within the context of the free particle spectral theory for Rarita-Schwinger fields.

A new technique in the field of probabilistic learning utilizes the pathwise conditioning of Gaussian processes to derive an explicit sampling formula for their posterior distributions given observed data. This formula is analogous to a kernel-based interpolation method but with a key distinction in handling unobserved input points: in traditional methods, unobserved inputs are treated as data points with unknown labels, whereas the new approach treats them as locations outside the observed data set. By incorporating a precise kernel function, the pathwise conditioning method facilitates the computation of an exact Gaussian process posterior without necessitating any data regression or prediction for unobserved inputs. The research demonstrates the connection between the pathwise conditioning technique and frequentist regression, as well as its link to Bayesian credible intervals. The study also showcases the efficacy of this approach in a range-based inference framework by providing a precise bound on the prediction error. The pathwise conditioning method is successfully evaluated in a series of experiments across regression, time series forecasting, and classification tasks, with results comparable to or surpassing existing state-of-the-art Gaussian process methods.

This paper proposes an enhanced Two-Ray model for the Internet of Aerial Things (IoAT), which accounts for the effects of both line-of-sight and diffuse signals. The model's initial development was limited by assuming that altitude differences between devices are negligible, a constraint that is not met by Internet of Things (IoT) applications involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The model has been expanded to consider the impact of varying altitudes between devices, specifically between unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground sensors within the IoAT framework. The model's validity was assessed through a comparison with measurements collected from 28 distinct pairs of sensors and antennas. The results demonstrate that the model's accuracy is within 2.5 dB of these measurements. The model was further evaluated in a UAV-based IoAT network, where it was used to optimize the placement of UAVs and ground sensors for maximum connectivity between the two systems. The results show that the model can be used to achieve a network connectivity of up to 100% even in scenarios with significant altitude differences between devices.

The DUNE experiment at Sanford Lab is designed to detect signals of various types, 
including long-term beam-generated signals, rare natural signals, and other types, 
utilizing a 10-kiloton liquid argon time projection detector. While its main goal is 
to study beam-generated signals, the same detector design offers significant 
advantages in detecting other types of signals at much lower levels. This work will 
focus on how the DUNE experiment can effectively detect proton decay signals, 
comparatively assessing its performance to that of other experiments like Super-Kamiokande 
and Hyper-Kamiokande.

A new framework, utilizing SHAP, has been developed to provide a framework for understanding the machine learning model's feature utilization during training. The approach, called SHAP-ML, enables real-time analysis of the model's dependence on its parameters and environmental factors as well as its internal structure, allowing for the assessment of the impact of external data variations on the model's performance. Furthermore, SHAP-ML can attribute the outcomes of the model to external data modifications post-hoc. The effectiveness of SHAP-ML is demonstrated through its application in understanding the effects of data augmentation techniques on the model's performance.

This paper presents a conceptual framework for Virtual Observatory (VO) architecture called VO2. This framework is designed to facilitate the development of highly adaptable and modular VO services that can seamlessly integrate multiple, disparate infrastructures as needed. A key aspect of VO2 is its recognition that essential functionalities within a VO are comprised of both core, universally applicable components and optional features that may or may not be relevant in specific contexts. Furthermore, VO2 emphasizes that even when present, optional features can be tailored to suit individual needs. Building upon this insight, VO2 introduces the concepts of "abstraction" and "instantiation" to describe variations arising from the application of these principles. A VO2 architecture implementing this framework is currently under development and is slated for public release as a reference model for VO services.

High-dimensional policy gradient parameter estimation is a major challenge in reinforcement learning due to its computational intensity. To address this issue, a novel variance reduction based experience replay framework, VRER, is proposed to enhance gradient estimation. By leveraging a general unbiased gradient estimator, VRER framework generalizes multiple existing gradient estimators, including those for bootstrapping, tree backup, and probability density matching. The framework also incorporates a common structure among these methods, enabling the development of more efficient algorithms. Theoretical analysis shows that VRER achieves faster convergence rates than prior methods under certain conditions. Experimental results on multiple benchmarks confirm that VRER yields superior performance and outperforms existing techniques.

Utilizing exceptional geometric flow properties, we prove the equivalence of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula. Our proof involves introducing a specific flow on the product of the complex Grassmannian and the complex projective space, which also underlies the construction of the superbosonization formula in relation to its applications in one- and two-dimensional systems. Furthermore, we extend the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to the context of higher-dimensional systems via a detailed mathematical representation.

In spatiotemporal learning, sufficient observation of temporal contexts is crucial and poses a challenge due to the limitations of most current models, which rely heavily on memory-based architectures that can only accommodate a limited number of past steps. To overcome this issue, a new model called Detail Context Block (DCB) is designed to efficiently incorporate detailed context information from multiple past steps within a compact framework. DCB's cross-steps interaction component utilizes a shared transformation for all steps, reducing computational overhead and making it well-suited for long-term contexts. Additionally, the model's cross-channel interaction component is used to combine feature maps from adjacent channels, enabling the effective incorporation of contexts at the channel level. The proposed Detail Context Block has been experimentally validated across various applications such as video classification, human action recognition, and traffic flow prediction, and has consistently demonstrated its ability to enhance model performance when compared to memory-less baselines.

Imperative languages have traditionally been analyzed using abstract interpretation, a method that infers properties of programs by bounding the effects of loops and recursion. In contrast, programming languages with a logical interface rely on model checking techniques, such as saturation, to infer properties. This paper presents a novel type system for the $\lambda_{IO}$ language, combining features of Haskell monads with dependent types, as a means to achieve memory safety in imperative programs via saturation. This process involves encoding $\lambda_{IO}$ as a dependent type theory within a higher-order logic, and then applying a saturation algorithm to derive a decision procedure for it. This type system can be used as an alternative to traditional model checking for memory management in imperative languages, offering the benefits of resource safety without the drawbacks of explicit type inference.

We propose a theoretical framework integrating heavy neutral leptons with mass less than 550 GeV to explain the observed anomaly in the decay of Kaon, specifically the $K^+ \rightarrow \pi^+ \nu \bar{\nu}$. Heavy neutral leptons, with properties similar to neutrinos, hold the key to lepton number violation and can be produced in large quantities at the LHC. A dedicated search for this process, combining data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC, could help establish or limit the parameters of this model.

This paper introduces a novel decoding approach for pre-transformed polar codes, specifically designed for cyclic redundancy check (CRC)-aided polar codes, with the ability to handle undecodable vectors and undetected errors. The proposed algorithm yields superior error rates when compared to traditional successive cancellation decoding, particularly in scenarios with limited CRC lengths and higher error probabilities. Notably, the new decoding method can be seamlessly integrated into existing SC decoding infrastructure without requiring significant modifications, making it easily implementable.

Nonlinear image combining techniques such as median and clipped-mean elimination of cosmic rays are used, but they maintain the cosmic ray signal and do not maintain a uniform point spread function across the detector. This results in a decrease in the precision of astrometric and photometric data when combining images. To address this, we have developed a logarithmic "clipping" image combination technique. This method, which we call "logclip", eliminates cosmic rays by taking a logarithm of the image and applying a threshold to the pixels, thereby preserving the astrometric and photometric accuracy of the images by maintaining a uniform point spread function across the detector. Our results show that the logclip method has a high accuracy in removing cosmic rays and maintaining the images' zero-point, astrometric and photometric calibrations.

A notched specimen is a classic representation of a pre-existing flaw in material that can lead to the initiation of fracture. In this study, the behavior of an elliptical notch in an elastic material when subjected to sharpening instability is investigated. This specific type of notch has been the focus of past research which found that it represents an optimal scenario for the destabilization due to its inherent ability to resist the effects of external loads. Consequently, the energy released as a result of the notch sharpening is sufficient to drive the propagation of a crack. Utilizing a combination of analytical and numerical models, this research aims to understand the relationship between the initial state of the notch and the energy released during the process of destabilization, as well as the effects of different material properties on this phenomenon.

We introduce the chordal Schramm--Loewner evolution (cSLE$_\kappa$) driven by general planar free fields, focusing on the specific cases of the Gaussian free field (GFF) and the Dyson--Schramm--Loewner (DSLE) field. Our work builds on prior research, including recent findings by Nahum--Schramm--Shen and Wang. We establish the cSLE$_\kappa$ driving process's relationship with the GFF and DSLE as the driving function's derivative within the respective complex function spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cSLE$_\kappa$ driven by the GFF develops imaginary, non-compact "loop" structures, referred to as "ghost loops," and prove that these "ghost loops" preserve conformal self-similarity. Lastly, we show that the cSLE$_\kappa$ driven by the Dyson--Schramm--Loewner field also develops these "ghost loops."

This study establishes a theoretical framework for the Navier-Stokes equations in a 2D/3D domain using maximum norm analysis. We derive a general existence theorem for 2D/3D Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded domain with $C^{1+}$. We also obtain a maximum norm estimate for the solution's derivatives up to order n, showing that it depends on the initial conditions' derivatives up to the same order. In 2D, we prove the existence of smooth solutions for all time for data in $C^{n+1+\alpha}$ and use this to demonstrate the existence of strong solutions for all time in $C^{n+1}$ when 3D.

A new consensus protocol, the CVQC (Verifiable Delay Function for Consensus) protocol, has been developed to enhance the security and efficiency of consensus through verification. This protocol employs a novel VDF computation that combines two modular exponentiations with a series of modular bit-wise XOR operations following each modular exponentiation. As a result, the complexity of each module in the CVQC protocol is significantly reduced, from $O(\lambda^{3/4})$ to $O(\lambda^{1/4})$. Furthermore, the CVQC protocol outperforms existing VDFs in various aspects, including verification speed ($O(\lambda^{3/4})$) and total computation cost ($O(\lambda^{3/2})$), while also achieving improved communication efficiency with a verification time of $O(\lambda^{3/4})$. The CVQC protocol has been formally proven secure and efficient, and its performance has been demonstrated through practical testing, showcasing its potential for real-world applications in consensus systems.

A blockchain-based system for supply chain tracking is enhanced through the integration of a novel consensus algorithm, LC4IoT. This algorithm is specifically tailored for Internet of Things devices and is designed to address high network latency, energy consumption, and hardware failure issues that arise in IoT settings.
